stem: A client with type 1 diabetes uses an insulin pump. Which teaching point is most important regarding interruption of pump insulin delivery?

options.A: Because pumps deliver rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting insulin continuously, prolonged interruption can allow hyperglycemia and ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis to develop quickly
options.B: A pump interruption is usually harmless for a full day because long-acting insulin remains under the skin
options.C: Insulin pumps eliminate the need to monitor glucose or respond to high-glucose alerts
options.D: If pump delivery stops, the client should avoid all insulin until the device can be professionally repaired

rationale: ADA 2026 Standards describe insulin pump therapy as continuous delivery of rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting insulin and specifically note the risk of rapid development of ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis when insulin delivery is interrupted. Pump users therefore need education on monitoring and an individualized backup/troubleshooting plan. Pumps do not create a long-acting subcutaneous insulin depot, do not eliminate glucose monitoring, and interruption is not a reason to withhold needed insulin. Therefore A is the best answer.
educational_objective: Teach insulin-pump users that interruption of rapid-acting insulin delivery can quickly lead to hyperglycemia and ketosis/DKA, requiring prompt recognition and use of the prescribed backup/troubleshooting plan.
source_document_title: 7. Diabetes Technology: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_version_date: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, published 2026
source_locator: Section 7 > Stand-alone Insulin Pumps and AID Systems: pumps deliver rapid-acting insulin throughout the day. Section 9 > Table 9.1 insulin pump therapy: basal delivery of ultra-rapid/rapid-acting insulin; disadvantage includes risk of rapid development of ketosis or DKA with interruption of insulin delivery
source_claim_supported: Insulin pumps provide continuous rapid/ultra-rapid insulin; interruption can rapidly lead to ketosis or DKA, making prompt monitoring and troubleshooting essential.

correction_summary: Replaced a generic advantage-of-pump question with a safety-critical current ADA construct: rapid-acting insulin delivery interruption and DKA risk. Avoided device-specific troubleshooting steps that vary by pump and individualized care plan.
audit_findings: A is directly supported by ADA 2026. B falsely assumes a long-acting insulin depot; C incorrectly eliminates monitoring; D dangerously advises withholding insulin. The item remains device-agnostic and does not invent an exact time-to-DKA threshold or universal backup dose. One clear best answer remains; independent adversarial second pass passed.
